subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Energy Use Feedback
description: A fast breakdown of Energy Use Feedback for builders.

hook.text: Opower sent homeowners a report comparing their energy use to their neighbors. High-use homes reduced consumption by 2%.

buildup.text: Social comparison reports work because people dislike being worse than their neighbors.

discovery.text: Allcott showed the effect persists even after reports stop. Social norms create new habits that outlast the original.

twist.text: Low-use households sometimes increase consumption after seeing they use less than neighbors.

climax.text: Energy feedback nudges are among the most cost-effective environmental policies.

punchline.text: Showing you use more than your neighbors saves more energy than guilt.

quiz.question: What is the boomerang effect in energy feedback?
options: High-use households increase consumption after getting reports
Low-use households increase consumption to match neighbors
Energy companies raise prices after high usage

details.summary: Energy use feedback provides households with real-time or periodic information about their energy consumption, often compared to neighbors. This visibility makes the abstract concept of energy use concrete and actionable, reducing consumption by 2 to 10 percent.
details.whyItMatters: Energy consumption is largely invisible. People cannot reduce what they cannot see. Making usage visible through smart meters, reports, and neighbor comparisons brings the hidden cost into awareness and enables targeted conservation.
takeaways: Real-time energy feedback reduces household consumption by 5 to 10 percent
Neighbor comparison reports reduce consumption by about 2 percent
Making invisible consumption visible is the foundation of conservation behavior

faq.question: How does comparing energy use to neighbors reduce consumption?
faq.answer: Social comparison activates descriptive norms. When people see they use more energy than neighbors, they feel motivated to reduce usage to match the norm. Opower's home energy reports leveraged this effect across millions of households.

faq.question: Can energy feedback increase consumption for some people?
faq.answer: Yes, the boomerang effect. People who discover they use less than neighbors may increase consumption toward the norm. Adding an injunctive norm, a smiley face for low usage, prevents this backfire by approving the desirable behavior.
